summary: Defines how the Extensible Provisioning Protocol is used to provision and manage host names stored in a shared registry. It specifies the command syntax and semantics for host objects. It obsoletes an earlier version and is an Internet Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5732 defines how EPP clients manage host-name records in a shared registry. These records can include IP addresses and can be linked to domain names.

subtitle: The EPP mapping for storing and managing host names in a shared registry.

tldr.problem: A shared domain registry needs a standard way for EPP clients to manage host names that domains can use, including nameserver addresses and status.
tldr.mechanism: The host mapping defines an XML object and applies EPP check, info, create, delete, and update commands to it. Host objects follow their superordinate domain for transfer and have no direct renewal operation.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5732 is an Internet Standard that replaces RFC 4932. It has no later update or replacement listed in the unit metadata.

today: RFC 5732 is an Internet Standard that obsoletes RFC 4932. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: The EPP Host Mapping
sections.content:
RFC 5732 defines an XML mapping for provisioning and managing Internet host names through version 1.0 of the Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP). It depends on RFC 5730 for the base EPP command and response structures.

A host object is a host name in a shared repository. A sponsoring client or the server can view and modify its attributes, subject to the mapping's rules.
sections.plainLanguage: A host object is a registry record for a host name. The mapping explains how an EPP client can check, create, read, update, or delete that record.

sections.title: Host Names and Parent Domains
sections.content:
A host name is normally subordinate to a domain name. For example, a host name may belong beneath a domain in the same repository. EPP actions that would break this relationship must be disallowed.

A repository can also store an external host name that does not belong to its own domain namespace. Whether a host is internal or external depends on the repository where it is used for delegation. A host used by another domain is still treated as internal when it belongs to the same repository.
sections.plainLanguage: A host record may be subordinate to a domain or external to the repository's domain namespace. The mapping uses that relationship to determine which actions are allowed.

sections.title: Host Attributes and Status
sections.content:
A host object has a name, at least one status value, and optionally IP addresses. The mapping requires host names to follow RFC 952 as updated by RFC 1123, and IP addresses to follow the IPv4 or IPv6 syntax cited by the RFC.

Statuses beginning with client are controlled by the sponsoring client; those beginning with server are controlled by the server. Other statuses are server-managed. Values such as linked describe associations, while pendingCreate or pendingUpdate show that an action has not yet completed.
sections.plainLanguage: Host records include status labels that show whether they are linked, restricted, or awaiting an action. The label's prefix identifies whether the client or the server controls it.

sections.title: Checking and Changing Host Records
sections.content:
check asks whether a name can be provisioned, and info retrieves its details. create adds a name and optional IP addresses. An address is required only when needed to create DNS glue records.

update can add or remove addresses and statuses or change the host name. delete removes a host, but the RFC says a host should not be deleted while other objects are associated with it because those objects may stop resolving.
sections.plainLanguage: EPP clients can check whether a host name is available, inspect it, create it, change it, or delete it. A client should check for associations before deleting a host.

sections.title: Transfers and Offline Review
sections.content:
The mapping does not define direct transfer or renewal commands for host objects. A host is transferred when its superordinate domain is transferred.

A server may hold a transform request for offline review. It returns result code 1001 and marks the host with a pending status, then notifies the client after the review through an EPP service message or another notification method.
sections.plainLanguage: A host does not have its own transfer or renewal operation. It follows its parent domain during a transfer, and a registry may review other changes before completing them.

sections.title: Names, Internationalization, and Security
sections.content:
The mapping specifies host-name syntax and allows IPv4 and IPv6 address values. EPP uses XML, which can carry Unicode; UTF-8 is recommended where XML parser encoding support differs.

This host mapping adds no security services. Security considerations are those in the base EPP specification and in the protocol layers used by EPP.
sections.plainLanguage: This mapping defines the data and commands for host records, but it does not add security protections. Those protections come from EPP and its underlying protocol layers.
